claims.text: The target alloy contains at least five elements, with titanium and nickel as the primary constituents.
The proposed initial composition contains approximately 40–50 at% Ti, 30–40 at% Ni, and at least three additional elements at 5–35 at% each.
The intervention is addition of 0.5–1.5 at% boron during alloy processing.
Adding 0.5–1.5 at% boron will cause in situ formation of finely dispersed boride precipitates.
The boride precipitates may include TiB2 or NiB.
The boride precipitates will be located principally at grain boundaries.
Boron encourages nucleation of stable boride phases in the proposed alloy.
Grain-boundary borides will pin grain boundaries and enhance grain-boundary cohesion.
The boride dispersion will impede dislocation motion during elevated-temperature deformation.
Boundary pinning and impeded dislocation motion will enhance elevated-temperature yield strength.
Enhanced grain-boundary stability will delay creep and reduce creep rate.
The boron-doped alloy will have higher yield strength and lower creep rate than an otherwise identical boron-free alloy.
The proposed operating and testing range is 600–800 °C under tensile or creep loading.
The 600–800 °C operating range is below temperatures at which new phase transformations could occur.
A controlled comparison will use identically processed boron-free and boron-added samples.
The hypothesis is falsified if the boron-added samples show less than a 15% increase in high-temperature yield strength, no reduction in creep rate, or no fine boride precipitates.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that each element must be present at 5–35 at%, but the proposed initial alloy contains 40–50 at% Ti and potentially up to 40 at% Ni.
The intervention introduces only 0.5–1.5 at% B, whereas the stated compositional boundary says each element must be present at 5–35 at%.
